verificationTemplate:
VERIFICATION

I, {petitioner_name}, the Petitioner / Revisionist herein, do hereby verify that the contents of paragraphs 1 to {lastParagraph} of the above revision petition are true and correct to my personal knowledge, and matters of legal submission are believed true on advice of counsel. No part is false and nothing material has been concealed.

Verified at {place} on this {date}.

Petitioner / Revisionist

promptInstructions: Draft a Criminal Revision Petition under appropriate provision: S.438 BNSS (HC's revisional jurisdiction; was S.397 CrPC for HC) or S.442 BNSS (Sessions Court's revisional jurisdiction).

BNSS provisions: S.438 — power of HC to call for records and examine; S.439 — corresponding power of Sessions; S.440 — power of Sessions Judge to refer to HC; S.441 — procedure on revision; S.442 — high court / sessions revision; S.443 — HC's power to order inquiry; S.527 — savings.
Note: S.438(2) BNSS — like S.397(2) CrPC — bar on revision against INTERLOCUTORY orders. Final / quasi-final orders only.

Test for interlocutory: Cite Madhu Limaye v. State of Maharashtra (1977) 4 SCC 551 — orders that decide important rights or affect ends of trial are NOT interlocutory; orders of pure procedural nature ARE interlocutory.
Cite Amar Nath v. State of Haryana (1977) 4 SCC 137 — definition of interlocutory order.
Cite Rajendra Kumar Sitaram Pande v. Uttam (1999) 3 SCC 134 — order of cognizance / summons is NOT interlocutory (revisable).

Cite Krishnan v. Krishnaveni (1997) 4 SCC 241 — bar of second revision under S.397(3) CrPC (now S.438(3) BNSS — bar to apply to both HC and Sessions in same case); HC can still exercise inherent jurisdiction.
REVISION IS SUPERVISORY, NOT APPELLATE. Scope: (i) correctness, (ii) legality, (iii) propriety of finding/sentence/order; or (iv) regularity of proceedings.
Cite Kaptan Singh v. State of MP (2011) 6 SCC 705 — revisional court has limited scope; cannot re-appreciate evidence like appellate court.
Cite State of Kerala v. Puttumana Illath Jathavedan Namboodiri (1999) 2 SCC 452 — perversity threshold for interference with factual findings in revision.
Cite Sanjay Kumar Rai v. State of UP (2021) — interlocutory orders bar, scope reiterated.

Grounds for revision: (a) jurisdictional error — court acted without jurisdiction or in excess; (b) illegality — order contrary to law or in disregard of mandatory procedure; (c) impropriety — order shocks conscience or breaches established norms; (d) factual perversity — only where finding is perverse, no evidence, or based on inadmissible evidence.
Para 1: Description of parties and status.
Para 2: Impugned order details — court, date, parties, case number.
Para 3: Brief factual background — proceedings below.
Para 4: Nature of impugned order — confirm it is NOT interlocutory; cite Madhu Limaye / Rajendra Kumar Sitaram Pande as applicable.
Para 5: Limitation — Art. 131 Limitation Act — 90 days from date of order/sentence (in case of conviction, from receipt of certified copy). If delayed, file companion S.5 Limitation Act application.
Para 6: Whether appeal lay — if appeal lies, revision generally not maintainable (per S.438(4) BNSS); revision is residual.
Para 7: Whether earlier revision was filed — bar under S.438(3) BNSS — only one revision (to either HC or Sessions, not both).
Para 8: Grounds of revision — itemise each ground with relevant precedent.
Para 9: Specific errors — paragraph-by-paragraph of impugned order with reasoning.
Para 10: Where lower court took cognizance / framed charge: refer to Bhushan Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2012) 5 SCC 424 — cognizance / summoning orders, judicial mind required.
Para 11: Where Magistrate erred in framing charges: cite Asim Shariff v. NIA (2019) 7 SCC 148; State of Maharashtra v. Som Nath Thapa (1996) 4 SCC 659 (charge framing principles).
Para 12: Where lower court misapplied BNS / Special Act ingredients — section-by-section analysis.
Para 13: Where there is procedural irregularity prejudicing fair trial.
Para 14: Interim stay sought — typically of further proceedings in trial court.
Para 15: Documents relied on — certified copies of impugned order, chargesheet, witness statements, lower court order sheet.
Note: In revision, evidence cannot be re-appreciated as appellate court would. Findings of fact stand unless perverse.

Choice of forum: Where impugned order by Magistrate — revision lies to Sessions (S.442) OR HC (S.438). Where impugned order by Sessions — revision lies only to HC. Strategic — Sessions revision may be quicker but limited; HC has wider scope and inherent powers (S.528).
Affidavit in support is mandatory.
Append Lawie disclaimer.

sections.description: Revisional powers of HC (replaces S.397 / S.401 CrPC)
Bar on revision against interlocutory orders
Bar on second revision — one revision only
Inherent powers of HC — concurrent / residual
Revision — 90 days from order / sentence (or from delivery of certified copy)

filing_checklist: Revision petition (original + copies as per court rules)
Certified copy of lower court order sheet / proceedings
Relevant chargesheet documents / lower court evidence
Condonation application if filed beyond 90 days
Disclaimer slip — Lawie drafting assistance acknowledged
validation_rules: impugned_order_date must be valid date in past
TIME-BAR CHECK: revision must be filed within 90 days of impugned_order_date else condonation needed
advocate_enrollment must match Bar Council format
